activities.title: The Vibration Hunt

materials.item: a sheet of paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Never touch a pressure cooker, a hot pan, a fan, a running mixer or a plug. Just listen to those. The side of a fridge is safe to touch.

schedule.what: Find 10 sounds at home. For each one, find what is vibrating.

activities.record: List 10 sounds. Next to each, write what is vibrating: string, skin, air, solid or body. Make a tally of each kind.

flow.do: Give your child the paper and pencil. Explain the hunt.
flow.say: We're vibration detectives. Every sound comes from something vibrating. Let's find ten sounds at home, and for each one, find what is vibrating.
flow.kid: You are a vibration detective! Find ten sounds. For each one, find what is vibrating.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Vibration Hunt. You hunt for sounds at home, and find the vibrating thing behind each one.

flow.do: 1. Walk around the home and listen. 2. For each sound, find the source. 3. If it is safe, touch it gently to feel the buzz. 4. Write each one down.
flow.say: Listen. What's that sound? Where does it come from? Can you feel it vibrating?
flow.kid: Walk and listen. Find where each sound comes from. Safe to touch? Feel it buzz. Write it down.
flow.parent: Good finds: the fridge humming (put a palm on its side), a ticking clock, a ceiling fan, a steel glass tapped with a spoon, your own throat, a bird outside, a door creaking, the pressure cooker whistle. Only listen to hot things, fans and mixers.

flow.do: Count how many of each kind you found: string, skin, air, solid, body. Make a tally.
flow.say: Which kind of vibration did we find most at home?
flow.kid: Count each kind. String, skin, air, solid, body. Which kind did you find most?
flow.think: Is anything in your home completely silent? How could you tell?

activities.context: This is a hunt around your home. You find ten sounds and, for each one, the thing that is vibrating to make it.

activities.title: The Coin Line: be the air molecules

materials.item: 6 coins of the same size, like ₹1 coins
a smooth table
family members or friends, if you have them, for the human line

activities.safety: In the human line, squeeze shoulders gently. No pushing.

schedule.what: Pass a push down a line of coins. Then pass a squeeze down a line of people. Then try it with gaps, like space.

activities.record: Draw the coin line, with an arrow showing the push travelling. Write one sentence: what travelled, and what stayed?

flow.do: 1. Lay 5 coins in a straight line on the table, each one touching the next. 2. Hold the 6th coin a hand's width away, in line. 3. Flick it so it slides into the end of the line.
flow.say: These coins are air molecules. Watch the coin at the far end when I flick this one.
flow.kid: Put 5 coins in a line, all touching. Flick a 6th coin into the end. Watch the coin at the far end!
flow.context: This is the first step of the Coin Line. Coins act as air molecules, to show how a sound is passed along.
flow.parent: The last coin shoots off and the middle ones hardly move. The coins must be the same size and touching. It works best on a smooth, hard table.

flow.do: 1. Space the 5 coins out, with a gap as wide as your palm between each one. 2. Flick the 6th coin in again, with the same gentle flick as before.
flow.say: Now the coins are far apart, like the few particles in space. What happens?
flow.kid: Now leave gaps between the coins. Flick again. Does the push reach the end?

ask.q: Why didn't the push reach the end this time?
good: The coins weren't touching.
The first coin slid a little and stopped before it reached the next one.

flow.parent: If a coin slides all the way to the next one, flick more gently or make the gaps wider.

flow.do: If you have 4 or more people: 1. Stand in a line, each with a hand on the next person's shoulder. 2. Everyone closes their eyes. 3. The first person gently squeezes the next shoulder. 4. When you feel a squeeze, pass it on. 5. The last person says 'Bang!'. 6. Time it, then try it with everyone standing far apart, not touching.
flow.say: We are air molecules. The first squeeze is the drum. Pass it on the moment you feel it.
flow.kid: Playing with others? Stand in a line. Pass a gentle shoulder squeeze down. The last one shouts 'Bang!'
flow.parent: A child alone can skip this step and repeat the coin line instead. Standing far apart, nobody can pass the squeeze. That is space.

flow.do: Talk about what travelled and what stayed.
flow.say: What went from one end to the other? Did any coin or person travel all the way?
flow.kid: What travelled down the line? Did any coin go all the way? What about sound in air?

check.q: In the coin line, what travelled from one end to the other?
options: The push, passed from coin to coin
check.why: The first coin stopped at the line. Only the push was passed along, coin to coin, and the last coin shot off. Sound in air works the same way. Picking 'the first coin' means thinking the source itself travels to your ear.

flow.think: Real air molecules are not in a neat line, and they never stop zooming about. How is the real air different from our coins?

activities.context: In this activity, coins and people act as air molecules. You pass a push along a line, to see how sound travels without any air moving across the room. Then you leave gaps, like in space.

activities.title: Kitchen Orchestra and the Jal Tarang

materials.item: 4 to 6 steel tumblers or glasses of the same size
a jug of water and a measuring cup
a steel spoon and a wooden spoon
things to tap: a steel plate, a clay matka or pot, a plastic box, a cold pressure cooker lid

activities.safety: Tap gently. Glass tumblers can crack if hit hard, so use steel tumblers if you have them. Wipe up any spills.

schedule.what: Tap things in the kitchen. Make a water-tumbler jal tarang and play a tune.

activities.record: Write which tumbler was highest and lowest, and how much water was in each.

flow.do: 1. Tap each kitchen thing with the steel spoon, then with the wooden spoon. 2. Listen to how long each one rings.
flow.say: Everything in the kitchen has its own voice. Let's listen to each one. What is vibrating?
flow.kid: Tap each thing with a spoon. Listen. Which rings longest? What is vibrating?
flow.context: This is the first step of Kitchen Orchestra. You tap kitchen things to hear their sounds, then make a jal tarang, an Indian instrument of bowls of water.
flow.parent: Steel rings long. Wood and plastic give a short knock. A clay matka sounds like a ghatam, the clay-pot drum from Tamil Nadu.

flow.do: 1. Line up 5 tumblers. 2. Pour water into them: 0, 50, 100, 150 and 200 ml. 3. Tap each one gently near the rim with the spoon.
flow.say: A jal tarang is a real Indian instrument, made of bowls with water in them. Let's make ours.
flow.kid: Put water in the tumblers: none, then a little more in each. Tap each one gently. Listen!

good: The one with the most water.
The full one.

flow.parent: When you tap a tumbler, the tumbler and the water vibrate together. More water means more to vibrate, so it vibrates more slowly and sounds lower. Blowing across a bottle works the other way, which can puzzle children. That belongs to Class 5.

flow.do: 1. Play the tumblers from emptiest to fullest. 2. Try to play a simple tune you know.
flow.say: Play them from emptiest to fullest. What happens to the note? Can you play a tune?
flow.kid: Tap from empty to full. Do the notes go up or down? Try to play a tune!

check.q: You tap tumblers with different amounts of water. Which one sounds lowest?
options: The fullest one, because more water makes it vibrate more slowly
check.why: The tapped tumbler and its water vibrate together. More water means more to move, so the vibration is slower and the note is lower. Picking 'the empty one' is a common guess, because empty things sound hollow and booming.

activities.context: In this activity, you tap things in your kitchen to hear what each one sounds like. Then you make a jal tarang, an Indian instrument of bowls with water in them.

activities.title: Rubber-band Veena

materials.item: an open tiffin box, plastic box or shoebox without its lid
4 rubber bands, some thin and some thick
a pencil

activities.safety: Don't stretch bands near your face. A band can snap and sting.

schedule.what: Pluck a band in the air, then over a box. Build a four-string veena.

activities.record: Draw your veena. Write which band was highest and which was lowest, and why.

flow.do: 1. Stretch one rubber band between your thumbs, in the air. 2. Pluck it. 3. Now stretch the same band around the open box. 4. Pluck it again.
flow.say: Listen to the band alone, then over the box. What changes?
flow.kid: Stretch a band between your thumbs. Pluck it. Now put it around the open box. Pluck again. Louder?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Rubber-band Veena. You build a string instrument from a box and rubber bands, and find out what the box does.
flow.parent: In the air, the band is very quiet. Over the box it is much louder. The box vibrates with the band and pushes more air. A veena's big wooden body works the same way. It is called a resonator.

flow.do: 1. Stretch all 4 bands around the open box, thinnest to thickest. 2. Slide the pencil under them near one end, as a bridge. 3. Pluck each one. 4. Look closely at a plucked band.
flow.say: Now we have four strings. Which band is highest? Look closely at one when you pluck it.
flow.kid: Put all four bands around the box. Slide a pencil under them. Pluck each one. Which is highest? Look at a plucked band.

ask.q: What does a plucked band look like?
good: Blurry.
It vibrates so fast it looks fat.

flow.do: 1. Make one band tighter. Hold the part of it under the box and pull it towards you, so the top part stretches more. Pluck the top part. 2. Press another band down onto the box with a finger, halfway along. Pluck the part between your finger and the pencil.
flow.say: A veena player tightens strings to tune them, and presses them on frets. Let's try both.
flow.kid: Make one band tighter. Pluck it. Now press a band down with a finger to make it shorter. Pluck again.

check.q: You make a band tighter or shorter. What happens to its note?
check.why: A tighter or shorter band vibrates faster. Faster vibration sounds higher. This is how veena and sitar players change notes. Picking 'lower' often comes from thinking a tight band is 'stronger', so it should boom.

flow.do: Play your veena. Try to play a short tune or a pattern of notes.
flow.say: Play us something. What is vibrating when you play?
flow.kid: Play a tune on your veena! What is vibrating: the band, the box, or both?
flow.think: The box made the band louder. Your throat, mouth and nose do something like this for your voice. Hum and feel your face and chest buzz.

activities.context: In this activity, you build a string instrument from a box and rubber bands. You find out what makes a string louder, higher and lower, like a real veena.

activities.title: Straw Shehnai

materials.item: plastic drinking straws, if you have any (paper straws go soggy)
scissors, used by a grown-up

activities.safety: A grown-up does all the cutting. Each person uses their own straw. Throw the straws away afterwards, or reuse them for crafts, not for drinking.

schedule.what: Make a straw reed. Make it buzz. Cut it shorter and hear the note change.

activities.record: Draw your straw shehnai and label the reed. Write what happened when it was cut shorter.

flow.do: 1. Flatten one end of the straw by pressing it hard with your teeth or fingers, for about 2 cm. 2. A grown-up cuts the flat end into a V shape, like a pointed arrow tip.
flow.say: A shehnai has a reed: two thin flaps that slap together when you blow. We'll make one from a straw.
flow.kid: Flatten one end of the straw. Ask a grown-up to cut it into a V shape.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Straw Shehnai. You make a straw into a reed instrument, like the shehnai played at Indian weddings.

flow.do: 1. Put the V end into your mouth, past the cut, about 2 cm in. 2. Close your lips around it. 3. Blow hard, without biting.
flow.say: Blow hard. It may take five or more tries. Move it a little further in or out each time.
flow.kid: Put the V end in your mouth. Close your lips. Blow hard! Keep trying. It takes practice.
flow.parent: Most children need several tries. If it won't buzz, flatten the V again, and press lips a little harder. Paper straws usually go soggy and don't work. When it works, it gives a loud, buzzy honk. Single-use plastic straws are no longer sold in India, so use any you already have. If you have none, skip this activity and try the Kitchen Orchestra instead.

flow.do: 1. While your child keeps blowing, a grown-up snips a bit off the far end of the straw. 2. Snip again. Listen each time.
flow.say: Keep blowing. Listen to what happens as the straw gets shorter.
flow.kid: Keep blowing! A grown-up will snip the end off. What happens to the note?

check.q: As the straw shehnai is cut shorter, what happens to its note?
check.why: The reed starts the vibration, but the air inside the straw sets the note. A shorter column of air vibrates faster, so the note goes higher. A bansuri works the same way when you uncover holes. Picking 'lower' means thinking less straw means less sound.

activities.context: In this activity, you make a reed instrument from a plastic straw. It shows how a shehnai's reed makes the air inside it vibrate.

setup.caption: 1. Flatten the end. A grown-up cuts it into a V.

setup.art: A child with cheeks puffed blowing into the V end of a straw, the two flaps drawn buzzing.
setup.caption: 2. Put the V in your mouth. Blow hard until it buzzes.

setup.art: A grown-up's scissors snipping a little off the far end of the straw while the child blows.
setup.caption: 3. Snip the end shorter while you blow. Listen.

activities.title: Animal Sound Makers

materials.item: a plastic comb
a fingernail or a card, like an old visiting card
a balloon
a floor and a quiet room

activities.safety: Blow up the balloon only part way. Rumble gently, never shout into anyone's ears.

schedule.what: Copy how a cricket, a frog and an elephant make their sounds.

activities.record: Draw one animal making its sound. Label the part that vibrates.

flow.do: 1. Run a fingernail or a card along the teeth of the comb, slowly, then fast. 2. Listen.
flow.say: A cricket makes its chirp like this. It rubs a hard scraper on one wing across a row of tiny teeth on the other wing.
flow.kid: Run a fingernail along a comb. Slow, then fast. That's how a cricket chirps, with its wings!
flow.context: This is the first step of Animal Sound Makers. You copy how a cricket, a frog and an elephant make their sounds, using things from home.

ask.q: What happened to the sound when you went faster?
good: It got higher.
The clicks joined into a buzz.

flow.do: 1. Blow up a balloon part way and pinch its neck. 2. Stretch the neck sideways so the air squeals out. 3. Try stretching it more and less.
flow.say: This squeal is like a frog's call. Air rushing past stretched rubber makes it vibrate. A frog's throat pouch swells like the balloon, which makes its call louder.
flow.kid: Pinch the balloon neck. Stretch it so it squeals. A frog's throat swells like a balloon when it calls!
flow.parent: Stretching the neck tighter usually makes the squeal higher, like tightening vocal folds.

flow.do: 1. Everyone lies down with a palm or cheek flat on the floor. 2. One person hums the lowest 'mmm' they can, with their chest close to the floor. 3. The others try to feel it through the floor.
flow.say: Elephants rumble so low that people can hardly hear it. Other elephants may feel it through their feet, kilometres away. Let's see if we can feel a hum through the floor.
flow.kid: Lie down. Put your hand on the floor. Someone hums very low. Can you feel it through the floor?
flow.parent: On a wooden or tiled floor, you can often feel a low hum faintly. If not, try a palm on a table while someone hums with their chest against it.

flow.do: Talk about why animals make sounds.
flow.say: A cricket, a frog and an elephant aren't making sounds for us. Why do you think they do it?
flow.kid: Why do crickets, frogs and elephants make sounds? Who are they talking to?

check.q: Why do most animals make their calls?
options: To find mates, keep in touch, warn others, or find food
check.why: Animals call for their own lives: to find each other, warn of danger, mark their home, or, like bats, find food by echoes. Picking 'to entertain people' puts people at the centre. Most animal calls have nothing to do with us.

activities.context: In this activity, you copy the way three animals make sound: a cricket's wings, a frog's throat pouch, and an elephant's low rumble that travels through the ground.

setup.caption: 1. Run a nail along a comb, like a cricket's wings.

setup.caption: 2. Make a balloon squeal, like a frog's call.

projects.title: My Instrument Concert

materials.item: things from home: boxes, tins, tumblers, rubber bands, balloons, straws, bottles, dried beans or rice, sticks
tape, string and scissors used by a grown-up
paper and colours for a concert poster

projects.safety: A grown-up does any cutting. Keep the concert at a comfortable loudness.

schedule.what: Choose a kind of instrument: string, skin, air or solid. Draw a design.
Build the instrument. Test it. Make one change to make it louder or change its note.
Give a concert for the family. Before each piece, explain what vibrates in your instrument.

projects.record: Keep the design drawing. Write what you changed on day 2, and why. Make a concert poster.

flow.do: 1. Choose a kind of instrument: string, skin, air or solid. 2. Draw a design and label the part that will vibrate. 3. List what you need.
flow.say: Every instrument in the world has a part that vibrates. Which kind will you build? Draw it first, like an inventor.
flow.kid: Choose: string, skin, air or solid. Draw your instrument. Label the part that vibrates.
flow.context: This is the first step of the 3-day My Instrument Concert project. You design, build and play your own instrument, then explain how it makes sound.

flow.do: 1. Build the instrument from the design. 2. Play it. 3. Ask: is it loud enough? Can it play more than one note?
flow.say: Let's build it and try it. What do you hear?
flow.kid: Build your instrument. Play it. Is it loud enough? Can it play two notes?
flow.wait: Come back to it the next day to finish.

flow.do: Make one change to improve it. For example, add a box to make it louder, or tighten or shorten something to change the note.
flow.say: Real instrument makers test and change, again and again. What one change could make yours better?
flow.kid: Make one change. A box for louder? Tighter or shorter for higher? Test it again.

check.q: Your rubber-band instrument is too quiet. Which change will help most?
options: Stretch the bands over a hollow box
check.why: A hollow box vibrates along with the band and pushes much more air, so the sound is louder. That is what a veena's body does. A thinner band changes the note, not the loudness. Paint changes how it looks, not how it sounds.

flow.do: 1. Make a poster for the concert. 2. Invite the family. 3. Before playing, explain what vibrates in your instrument. 4. Play.
flow.say: Welcome to the concert! Before you play, tell us what is vibrating.
flow.kid: It's your concert! Tell everyone what vibrates in your instrument. Then play!
flow.think: Every instrument in the world, from a veena to a drum to a flute, is a way of making something vibrate. What would you invent next?

projects.context: In this 3-day project, you design and build your own instrument, then play it in a family concert and explain what vibrates.

challenges.title: One Band, Biggest Sound
challenges.problem: Using just one rubber band, make the loudest sound you can by plucking it.
constraints: You may use anything else from home to hold it or put it on.
No shouting, no banging, no phones: only the plucked band.
materials: things from home: boxes, tins, tumblers, a tiffin, a thali, a cardboard tube, a plastic bucket
general: Stretch the band over an open box. The box vibrates with it and pushes more air.
Try a bigger hollow thing, like a bucket or a big tin.
Stretch it tighter, so it springs back harder.
creative: Press the ends of the stretched band against a table top or a door while you pluck it. The whole table or door becomes a sounding board.
A veena uses a big hollow body, and sometimes a second gourd at the top. Could two boxes help?
Put your ear against the box while someone plucks. Does it sound louder through the box than through the air?
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own way. Draw it, try it, and ask someone to judge which is loudest from across the room.

flow.do: 1. Stretch the band between your thumbs and pluck it. 2. Ask someone across the room if they can hear it.
flow.say: This is how quiet one band is on its own. Your challenge: make it as loud as you can.
flow.kid: Pluck the band in the air. Quiet, isn't it? Your job: make it as loud as you can!
flow.context: This is the first step of One Band, Biggest Sound. You start by hearing how quiet a single plucked band is.

flow.do: List three ideas before trying any.
flow.say: Before trying anything, let's think. What could make the band push more air?
flow.kid: Think first, like an engineer. Draw or write three ideas.

flow.do: 1. Try each idea. 2. The judge stands across the room and says which is loudest.
flow.say: Try each idea. Our judge will decide which is loudest.
flow.kid: Try each idea. Ask your judge: which is loudest?
flow.parent: Hollow boxes, tins and buckets help a lot. Pressing the band's ends against a table or a cupboard door often works very well, because the big flat surface pushes lots of air.

flow.do: Read the usual and the creative ideas together. Then invent a new one.
flow.say: Here are some usual ideas, and some creative ones. Can you beat them?
flow.kid: Look at the ideas. Now invent your own. Can you beat them?

check.q: Why does a band sound louder over a hollow box?
options: The box vibrates too, and pushes much more air
The box makes the band vibrate faster
The box stores up the sound
check.why: The band alone is thin, so it pushes very little air. The box's big sides vibrate along with it and push much more air. Picking 'faster' mixes up loudness with pitch. Picking 'stores up' means thinking of sound as a thing that can be kept.

challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You must make one plucked rubber band as loud as possible, by finding what helps it push more air.

setup.caption: 2. Try it over boxes, tins and buckets.

setup.caption: 3. Ask a judge across the room which is loudest.

challenges.title: A Doorbell for Someone Who Cannot Hear
challenges.problem: Design a doorbell for a person who is deaf. When someone arrives, the person inside must know, without hearing anything.
constraints: It must work without the person hearing a sound.
The visitor must be able to work it from outside the door.
materials: a long piece of string or thread, a bell or a spoon, a tin, a balloon, a torch, a cloth, tape
general: A light that flashes, like a torch switched on by the visitor.
Something that moves where the person can see it, like a cloth flag pulled by a string.
A vibration they can feel, like a string tied to a chair or to the bed that the visitor tugs.
creative: Evelyn Glennie, a great Scottish drummer, is profoundly deaf. She plays barefoot, to feel the music through the floor. Could a knock on the floor work as a doorbell?
Many deaf people use phones that vibrate in their pocket. Could a family use a vibrating phone as a doorbell?
A vibration travels well along a tight string. A string from the door to the person's chair could carry a tug.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own doorbell. Draw it, build a model, and test it with someone who closes their eyes and covers their ears.

flow.do: Talk about the problem together.
flow.say: Many people can't hear a doorbell. Some were born deaf, and many grandparents slowly lose their hearing. How could they know someone is at the door?
flow.kid: Some people cannot hear a doorbell. How could they know someone has come?
flow.context: This is the first step of the doorbell challenge. You design a doorbell for a person who cannot hear.

flow.do: List three ideas: one you can see, one you can feel, and one other.
flow.say: Sound is a vibration. People can also feel vibrations, or see things move. Let's list three ideas.
flow.kid: Think of three ideas. One you can see. One you can feel. One more.

flow.do: 1. Build a model of your best idea. 2. Test it: the tester sits with eyes closed and ears covered. 3. The 'visitor' rings it.
flow.say: Let's test it. The tester closes their eyes and covers their ears. Did they notice the visitor?
flow.kid: Build it. Test it on someone with eyes closed and ears covered. Did they notice?
flow.parent: A string tied to the tester's chair or wrist and tugged from the door works well. So does a cushion or table they rest a hand on, which the visitor knocks. Ask the tester what it felt like.

flow.do: Read the usual and the creative ideas together. Then improve your design.
flow.say: Evelyn Glennie says hearing is a kind of touch. What do you think she means?
flow.kid: A deaf drummer says hearing is a kind of touch. What do you think she means?

check.q: Evelyn Glennie is deaf, yet she plays drums. How does she feel the music?
options: She feels the vibrations through her body and the floor
She can't feel it at all
She just watches the other players
check.why: Sound is a vibration, and vibrations can be felt as well as heard. She plays barefoot to feel them through the floor. Picking 'can't feel it at all' means thinking sound is only for ears.

challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You invent a doorbell that a person who is deaf can notice, using what you know about vibrations.

quiz.p: What do all sounds have in common?
opts: They all start with something vibrating
quiz.why: Every sound starts with a vibration. Picking 'loud' forgets whispers and rustles. Picking 'machines' forgets voices, birds and rain.

quiz.p: You pluck a rubber band and it looks blurry. Then you touch it. What happens?
opts: The sound stops, because the band stops vibrating
quiz.why: Touching the band stops its vibration, and the sound stops at once. Picking 'louder' means thinking a touch adds to the sound.

quiz.p: In a bansuri flute, what vibrates to make the sound?
quiz.why: In a wind instrument, the column of air inside vibrates. The fingers only cover and uncover holes to change the note. Picking 'the bamboo only' is a common guess, because the flute is what we see.
Like all drums, the mridangam's stretched skins vibrate when struck. The wood and straps hold the skins tight.

quiz.p: In the Twanging Ruler experiment, which length sticking out gave the highest sound?
quiz.why: The shortest piece vibrates fastest, so it sounds highest. At 25 cm it wobbles so slowly that you hardly hear it. Picking 'longest' often means thinking bigger is always higher.

quiz.p: A drum is played across a room. What reaches your ear?
opts: Air from the drum, flying across the room
A pattern of pushes passed from molecule to molecule
quiz.why: No air flies across the room. Each molecule moves back and forth a tiny distance and pushes the next. Only the pattern travels to you. Picking 'air flying across' is the most common mistake about sound.

quiz.p: In the Coin Line, why did the flick stop working when the coins had gaps?
opts: The coins were too far apart to pass the push on
quiz.why: With gaps, the moving coin stopped before it reached the next one. In space, molecules are so far apart that sound can't be passed on either.

quiz.p: Why could astronauts on the Moon not talk to each other through the air?
opts: There is no air on the Moon to carry the sound
quiz.why: With no air, there is nothing to pass the vibration from one helmet to the other. They used radio. Radio waves are the same kind of wave as light, and need no air.

quiz.p: What makes a tabla ring with a clear note instead of a thud?
opts: The black syahi patch on its skin
quiz.why: The heavy syahi changes how the skin vibrates, so its vibrations fit together into one note. C.V. Raman and Sivakali Kumar explained this in 1920. Drum makers had invented it long before.

quiz.p: Why does a veena have a big hollow wooden body?
opts: It vibrates with the strings and makes the sound much louder
It holds the musician's music books
It makes the veena easier to carry
quiz.why: A thin string pushes little air. The big body vibrates along with it and pushes far more. This hollow part is called a resonator.

quiz.p: How does a cricket make its chirp?
opts: By rubbing a scraper on one wing against tiny teeth on the other
quiz.why: Crickets rub their wings together. The wings vibrate and make the chirp. Picking 'with its mouth' comes from thinking all animal sounds are like our voices.

quiz.p: Elephants call with rumbles too low for people to hear. What is sound this low called?
quiz.why: Infrasound is too low for us. Ultrasound is too high for us, like bat squeaks. Katy Payne discovered elephant infrasound in 1984.

quiz.p: Scientists recorded clicks from thirsty tomato plants in 2023. Which is true?
opts: The clicks are real, but whether animals listen is still unknown
The plants are talking in words
quiz.why: The clicks were carefully recorded. What they mean, and whether anything listens, is still open. Saying what we don't know yet is part of good science.

applications: Every musical instrument, from a veena to a drum kit, is a way of making something vibrate.
Loudspeakers and earphones have a thin cone that vibrates to make sound.
Microphones have a thin skin that vibrates when sound hits it, like a tiny drum.
Phones buzz in your pocket because a tiny motor inside shakes them.
Doctors use ultrasound, sound too high to hear, to see babies growing inside the mother.
Ships use sonar, sending out sound and listening for echoes, to find the sea floor and fish.
Engineers listen to machines and bridges. A change in their vibration can warn of a crack.
Scientists listen to the Sun's vibrations to learn what is happening deep inside it.
Earthquake scientists record the ground's vibrations to find where a quake started.
Speech therapists help people whose vocal folds are hurt to find their voice again.
Hearing aids and cochlear implants help people who are deaf or hard of hearing.
Wildlife scientists record animal calls to count frogs, birds and whales without disturbing them.

open_questions.q: Why do people make music at all?
open_questions.why_open: Every culture has music. Scientists have several ideas: bonding groups, calming babies, or a side effect of language. None is proven.

open_questions.q: Do any animals listen to the clicks of thirsty plants?
open_questions.why_open: The clicks were only recorded in 2023. Nobody has yet shown that any animal uses them.

open_questions.q: How much do elephants understand from rumbles they feel through the ground?
open_questions.why_open: We know they can feel them. What they learn from them, like who is calling and why, is still being studied.

open_questions.q: Why do humpback whales sing, and why do whole groups change their song together?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have ideas, mostly about finding mates, but nobody knows for sure.

open_questions.q: Why do some sounds, like rain or a lullaby, calm us, while a scratch on a board makes us shiver?
open_questions.why_open: Some of it is about the vibrations, some about the brain and what we have learned. How it all fits is not understood.

open_questions.q: What did the very first sound in the universe 'sound' like?
open_questions.why_open: Sound waves rang through the young universe, and we see their pattern. What came before them, and whether there was a 'first' sound, is not known.
Even in empty space, there are a few particles, and everything is always jiggling. Whether perfect silence can exist depends on what we mean by silence.

maths.problem: In the Twanging Ruler experiment, you tested the ruler with 5 cm sticking out, then 10, 15, 20 and 25 cm. How many centimetres did you add each time? How many times longer was the 25 cm piece than the 5 cm piece?
maths.answer: You added 5 cm each time. The 25 cm piece was 5 times as long as the 5 cm piece.
maths.explain: The lengths go 5, 10, 15, 20, 25. Each one is 5 more than the one before. To compare the longest with the shortest, divide: 25 divided by 5 is 5. You can check: 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 25. The longest piece was 5 times as long, and it shook much more slowly.
maths.context: This is about the Twanging Ruler experiment. You press a ruler on a table so part of it sticks out, flick the end, and listen. Then you change how much sticks out.

answer_chart.title: How much of the ruler stuck out in each try

maths.why_maths: A fair test changes one thing in equal steps. Measuring the steps, and comparing the longest with the shortest, tells us how much we changed it.

maths.problem: For the jal tarang, you poured water into 5 tumblers: 0, 50, 100, 150 and 200 ml. If you added a 6th tumbler following the same pattern, how much water would it need? How much water did all 5 tumblers hold together?
maths.answer: The 6th tumbler would need 250 ml. All 5 held 500 ml together.
maths.explain: Each tumbler has 50 ml more than the one before. So the next one is 200 + 50 = 250 ml. To find the total, add them: 0 + 50 + 100 + 150 + 200. Pair them up: 50 + 150 = 200, and 0 + 200 = 200. That makes 400, plus the 100 in the middle, which is 500 ml. That is half a litre.
maths.context: This is about the Kitchen Orchestra activity. You make a jal tarang, an Indian instrument, from tumblers with different amounts of water. The fuller ones sound lower.

answer_chart.title: Water in each jal tarang tumbler

maths.why_maths: Instrument makers tune by changing things in steady steps. Spotting the pattern tells you how to add the next note, and how much water you need.

maths.problem: In the human line, 8 people passed a shoulder squeeze from one end to the other. It took 4 seconds. On average, how long did each person take to pass it on?
maths.explain: 4 seconds were shared between 8 people. 4 divided by 8 is a half. Check: two people take one second, because a half and a half make one. So 8 people take 4 seconds. Sound is far faster. In one second it travels about 343 metres through the air.
maths.context: In the Coin Line activity, family members stood in a line and passed a gentle shoulder squeeze along, like air molecules passing on a sound.

answer_chart.title: People in the line and time taken, at half a second each

maths.why_maths: Sharing the total time between the people tells us how quick each pass was. That helps us compare our slow human line with real sound.

maths.problem: In the Vibration Hunt, a child found these sounds: fridge (solid), clock (solid), crow (body), fan (air), steel glass (solid), own voice (body), pressure cooker whistle (air), door creak (solid), sister singing (body), toy guitar (string). Make a tally of each kind. Which kind was found most?
maths.answer: Solid: 4. Body: 3. Air: 2. String: 1. Skin: 0. Solid things were found most.
maths.explain: Go through the list and make one tally mark for each sound under its kind. Fridge, clock, steel glass and door are solid: 4. Crow, own voice and sister are body: 3. Fan and whistle are air: 2. The toy guitar is string: 1. No drums, so skin is 0. The biggest count is 4, for solid.
maths.context: This is about the Vibration Hunt. You find sounds at home, and for each one you find what kind of thing is vibrating: a string, a skin, air, a solid thing or a body.

answer_chart.title: Sounds found in the Vibration Hunt, by what was vibrating

maths.why_maths: A hunt gives you a messy list. Sorting it into a tally shows at a glance which kind of sound source is most common in your home.

roots.context: We have been learning that every sound starts with a vibration, and that the air passes it on from molecule to molecule. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Flick a coin into a line of coins, and only the far coin shoots off. Sound travels the same way: no air travels from the drum to you. Each molecule only pushes its neighbour, and the push travels on. So what reaches your ear is the drum's movement, not any part of the drum.
deep_truth.habit: We say a sound 'comes' to us from the drum, as if it were a thing flying across the room. But no air and no part of the drum makes the journey. What travels is a movement, passed on by things that each stay where they are.
deep_truth.evidence: In the coin line, the middle coins hardly moved, yet the last coin shot away. In a real sound wave, each air molecule moves back and forth less than the width of a hair, yet the sound crosses a room in a hundredth of a second.

three.who_am_i: Your voice is your own vocal folds vibrating. When you hum, that movement is passed on through the air of the whole room.
three.what_is_life: Crickets, frogs, elephants and bats find each other, warn each other and hunt by sound. Many of their calls are too high or too low for us, and most are not meant for us at all.
three.what_is_this_world: Sound travels wherever there is a medium to carry it: air, water, wood, even the hot gas inside the Sun. Where there is nothing, as in space, there is silence.

roots.thread: One tap on a tabla starts one vibration. The air passes it on to billions of molecules, and it reaches every ear in the room: yours, your mother's and the cat's. Each ear receives the same movement, yet no molecule travelled from the drum to anyone. DeepKids believes the world is joined in this way: what happens in one place is passed on and shared by everything around it.

science.text: In a sound wave in air, each molecule moves back and forth far less than the width of a hair, while the wave itself travels about 343 metres every second.
When the universe was young, sound waves rang through its hot, thick gas. Their pattern can still be seen in the faint glow left over from that time, and in how galaxies are spread across the sky.

practice.title: The bee hum and the silence after
practice.say: This is called bhramari, the bee breath. It is described in an old yoga book, the Hatha Yoga Pradipika. Sit comfortably and close your eyes. Gently press the flaps of your ears closed with your thumbs. Breathe in through your nose. Now breathe out slowly while humming 'mmmm', like a bee. Feel where the hum is: your lips, your face, your head, your chest. Do it three times. Then take your hands away and sit very still. Listen to the sounds around you. Notice how each one starts, and then fades. What is still there when the hum has gone?
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Press your ear flaps shut with your thumbs. Breathe in. Hum like a bee as you breathe out. Feel it buzz in your head. Do it three times. Then sit still and listen to the silence.

how_we_found_out.story: Around 1640, in Rome, Gasparo Berti made a tall tube with almost no air at the top. He fixed a small bell inside the empty part and made it ring from outside. People could still hear it. So the scholar Athanasius Kircher decided that sound does not need air at all. In 1660, in England, Robert Boyle tried a more careful test. His assistant, Robert Hooke, had built a pump that could suck the air out of a glass jar. Boyle hung a ticking watch inside the jar and listened as the air was pumped out. The ticking grew fainter and fainter. When he let the air back in, the ticking came back. So sound needs air, or another medium, to travel. Later scientists saw what had gone wrong in Rome. Berti's bell was fixed to the tube, so its vibration could travel through the metal and glass. Some air was probably left inside too. Today we know that space, with almost no air, carries no sound at all.
how_we_found_out.who: Gasparo Berti and Athanasius Kircher in Rome, then Robert Boyle and Robert Hooke in England
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Sound does not need air. Berti's bell seemed to ring in an empty tube, but its vibration escaped through the tube itself. Boyle's watch went quiet as the air was pumped out, and could be heard again when the air came back.
